summary: Aleksandra Turek is an Indologist who earned her M.A. and Ph.D. from the University of Warsaw (1996–2009). She became an assistant professor at the University of Warsaw in 2010.

Aleksei Davydovich Litman (1923–1992) was a scholar of philosophy and Indology who studied at Moscow State University (~1945–1950). He served as Secretary at the Academy of Sciences of Tajikistan (1951–1956) and joined the Institute of Oriental Studies in 1957.

Aleksei Dyakov (1896–1974) worked in Indology and history/archaeology. He studied at Moscow State University (1913–1914, ~1916–1921) and Tomsk State University (1914–1919), later becoming a professor at the Institute of Oriental Studies in 1950.

Aleksei Osipovich Ivanovskii (1863–1903) was a sinologist and tibetologist who studied at Saint Petersburg State University from 1881 under Vasily Vasiliev, Aleksey Pozdneev, and Ivan Pavlovich Minaev. In 1894, he succeeded Sergey Georgiyevsky.

Indologist and linguist Aleksej Petrovič Barannikov (1890–1952) studied at Kyiv University under Friedrich Knauer, and under Sergey Oldenburg and Fyodor Shcherbatskoy. He taught at Saint Petersburg State University and directed the Institute of Oriental Manuscripts (1938–1940, 1946–1952).

Aleksej Stepanovič Barhudarov (1927–2001) was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Saint Petersburg State University (~1945–1950). He worked at the Institute of Oriental Studies (1953–1971) and joined the Institute of Linguistics in 1971.

Aleksey Sergeevich Sukhochev (1928–2000) was an Indologist who studied at Moscow State University (~1952–1957). In 1956, he became a scientific researcher (naučnyj sotrudnik) at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
Aleksey Shakhmatov studied under Filipp Fedorovich Fortunatov and Theodor Korsch circa 1883–1887.

Alessandro Giudice is an Indologist who studied at the University of Pisa and the University of Cagliari. He held cultore della materia roles at Pisa and Cagliari, and posts at the University of Munich and Göttingen Academy of Sciences (attested 2026).

Alessandro Graheli specializes in Indology and philosophy. He has held positions as university assistant at the University of Vienna (attested 2022), principal investigator at the IKGA (attested 2022), and assistant professor at the University of Toronto (attested 2026).
Alessandro Veniero worked in linguistics and Indology. He served as a professor at the University of Catania in 1917 and as principal at Liceo di Macerata from 1918 to 1919.

Alex McKay (born 1953) is a tibetologist and historian who earned his PhD from SOAS University of London (ended 1995). He has held fellowships at SOAS, the International Institute for Asian Studies, and University College London.

Alex Watson works in Indology and philosophy. Educated at Oxford and SOAS, he was supervised by Alexis Sanderson and Harunaga Isaacson and taught by Ernst Steinkellner. He held posts at Oxford, Harvard, and Ashoka University (attested 2018–2020).

Alex Wayman (1921–2004) was a scholar of Buddhist studies, Indology, and Tibetology. He studied at UCLA, UC Berkeley, and Nava Nalanda Mahavihara, and held academic posts at UC Berkeley, Wisconsin-Madison, and Columbia University (1966–1991).

Alexander B. Nicholson (1848–1906) was a scholar of Indology and linguistics. After studying at Princeton Theological Seminary, he served as principal of Cedar Hill School and held posts at Queen's University of Ireland, becoming professor in 1902.

Alexander Berzin (born 1944) is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. Educated at Rutgers, Princeton, and Harvard under Masatoshi Nagatomi, he co-founded the translation bureau at the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives (~1972–1979).

Alexander Coburn Soper (1904–1993) was an art historian of Japan and China. He studied at Hamilton College and Princeton University (Ph.D. ~1937–1944), held professorships at Bryn Mawr and NYU, and edited Artibus Asiae (1958–1993).

Alexander Cunningham (1814–1893) was an archaeologist and Indologist who studied at Addiscombe Military Seminary and under James Prinsep. He founded the Archaeological Survey of India, serving as its Archaeological Surveyor (1861–1865) and Director-General (1871–1885).

Alexander Duff (1806–1878) was a scholar in religious studies and history/archaeology. He studied at the University of St Andrews (~1821–1829) and the University of Aberdeen, and he taught Krishna Mohan Banerjee.

Alexander Duncan Campbell (1786–1857) worked in Indology and linguistics. He served on the Board of Superintendence at the College of Fort St. George in 1816 and was active in the Madras Literary Society.
